opus-5.5.text:
I think people often frame it as a dichotomy, and I don't really see it that way. End-to-end training and modularity are actually quite compatible. You can have a system that is structured into components — perception, behavior prediction, planning — with well-defined intermediate representations between them, and still train the whole thing end to end, so gradients flow from the downstream objectives back into the earlier parts of the stack.

The question is really what you gain from each. End-to-end training lets you optimize for what you actually care about, which is driving well, rather than for proxy metrics at each stage. It lets information that matters downstream be preserved and shaped by the final task, instead of being thrown away at some hand-designed interface. That's powerful, and as models and data scale, we've seen the benefits keep growing.

But modularity and structured intermediate outputs give you things that matter a lot in a safety-critical domain. They give you interpretability: you can inspect what the system believes about the world, what objects it sees, what it thinks other agents will do. They give you the ability to validate and test pieces independently, to inject priors and constraints, to apply additional supervision at intermediate stages, which helps a lot with sample efficiency. And they make it much easier to diagnose failures and to build a convincing safety case, which is ultimately what you need to deploy at scale without a human behind the wheel.

So my view is that the right design is a hybrid: models that are trained end to end, potentially very large and with foundation-model-style pretraining, but that still expose meaningful structured representations and can be supervised and evaluated at those points. You get the optimization benefits of end-to-end learning while keeping the engineering, validation, and safety benefits of a modular system. I'd say the field is converging on something like that, rather than one paradigm simply winning over the other.

r001.rationale: It says the system can have components with intermediate representations and still be trained end to end, with gradients flowing from downstream objectives back through earlier parts.

r002.rationale: The response describes end-to-end training across the whole system; it does not state that training can span only part of the stack or stop short of sensors to controls.

r003.rationale: It favors a hybrid with potentially large models, but does not say that consolidating the stack into fewer, larger components simplifies development.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a bit of a false dichotomy, honestly, and it's one of the more interesting debates in the field. People tend to frame it as "either you build a big monolithic network that goes from sensors to steering, or you build a pipeline of modules—perception, prediction, planning—with hand-designed interfaces between them." And I'd say the reality at Waymo, and I think increasingly across the industry, is somewhere in between, and it's deliberately so.

Let me unpack that a little. The appeal of end-to-end is obvious. If you train the whole system jointly against the final objective—drive well, drive safely—then the intermediate representations get optimized for what actually matters for driving, rather than for some proxy a human engineer decided on. A classic example: in a modular system, you might have a detector that outputs 3D boxes, and the planner consumes those boxes. But a box is a lossy abstraction. It throws away information about the shape of an object, about uncertainty, about things that aren't well described as boxes at all—debris, a gate, a plastic bag blowing across the road. End-to-end training lets the gradient flow back and tell the earlier stages, "actually, the thing you're losing here matters downstream."

And there's a second appeal, which is scale. End-to-end systems lend themselves to being trained on enormous amounts of data with relatively little labeling, and we've seen in the broader ML world what happens when you can scale that way.

But modularity has very real benefits too, and I think people sometimes underweight them because they're less glamorous. The first is interpretability and debuggability. When something goes wrong—and in driving, something will go wrong—you need to be able to answer: did we not see it, did we see it and mispredict what it would do, or did we see and predict it correctly and then make a bad decision? Those have completely different fixes. A system with meaningful intermediate representations lets you ask that question. A truly opaque end-to-end system makes it very hard.

The second is validation and safety. We have to be able to make statements about the behavior of the system with some rigor. Having interfaces where you can inject structure, enforce constraints, test components in isolation, build targeted evaluations—that's incredibly valuable. It's much harder to reason about the safety of a system where every behavior is an emergent property of a single giant model.

And the third, which I think is underappreciated, is data efficiency on rare events. Driving has this very long tail. If your only signal is the final driving outcome, then learning what to do about, say, an emergency vehicle approaching from behind at an unusual angle requires seeing enough examples of that whole situation. Whereas if you have a notion of "emergency vehicle" as an intermediate concept, you can supervise it, you can reason about it, you can compose it with other knowledge. Structure is a form of prior, and priors are how you deal with the long tail.

So the way I think about it is: end-to-end is about how you train, and modularity is about how you structure the representation. Those are not mutually exclusive. You can have a system with meaningful modules—perception, behavior prediction, planning—and still train them jointly, so that gradients flow across the boundaries. You can have intermediate representations that are learned rather than hand-specified, but that are still inspectable and that you can still supervise when you want to. The question isn't "modules or no modules," it's "what should the interfaces look like, how rich should they be, and which ones should be fixed versus learned."

And my view is that that answer evolves over time. Early on, when you don't have much data and the models are weaker, you want more structure—you're encoding your knowledge as engineers because the model can't learn it. As you get more data and more capable models, you can relax that structure, let more of it be learned, and make the interfaces richer. We've gone through exactly that progression. Things that used to be hand-coded are now learned; interfaces that used to be very narrow are now much wider. But we haven't thrown out the idea of interfaces entirely, and I don't think we will, because the reasons for having them—interpretability, validation, handling the long tail—don't go away just because your model gets bigger.

The other thing I'd add is that foundation models change this conversation somewhat. Once you have large models that have broad world knowledge, you can start using them as a sort of backbone that feeds many of these components, and that again blurs the line. The modularity becomes less about separate networks and more about separate heads, separate supervision signals, separate ways of probing a shared representation. That's, I think, a pretty healthy place to land.

r001.rationale: The response says meaningful modules can be trained jointly, with gradients flowing across their boundaries.

r002.rationale: It discusses joint training across modular boundaries but does not state that end-to-end training can cover only a portion of the stack.

r003.rationale: It says structure may be relaxed as models grow more capable, but does not say that consolidating components simplifies development.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think end-to-end training and modularity are mutually exclusive. They describe different aspects of a system. Modularity is about how you structure the problem, and end-to-end training is about how you optimize the components together.

You can have a system with components for perception, prediction, and planning, and still train across those boundaries. That’s valuable because you want perception and prediction to support good driving decisions, rather than just perform well on their individual metrics.

At the same time, structure gives you a way to understand what the system is doing, diagnose failures, and evaluate intermediate outputs. The challenge is to make sure those interfaces don’t discard information that matters downstream. So I see the goal as combining useful structure with joint optimization, rather than choosing between a modular system and an end-to-end system.

r001.rationale: The response says components can be trained across boundaries and optimized jointly, but does not clearly state that gradients pass across module boundaries.

r002.rationale: It describes training across perception, prediction, and planning, but does not say end-to-end training can be limited to part of the stack without spanning sensors to controls.

r003.rationale: The response does not say that combining the stack into fewer, larger components simplifies development.

sol-6.1.text:
I think end-to-end training and modularity are actually quite compatible. They address different questions. Modularity is about how you structure the system, while end-to-end training is about how you optimize it.

You can have a system with perception, prediction, and planning components, but train those components jointly so that the information they produce is useful for the ultimate driving task. That matters because improving a perception metric in isolation doesn’t necessarily improve driving. You want the training signal to reflect what the vehicle needs to do.

At the same time, structure is valuable. It gives you intermediate representations you can inspect, helps you understand failures, and lets you bring supervision to different parts of the system. So I wouldn’t frame it as choosing between a modular system and an end-to-end system. The interesting question is what structure you build in, and how you train across those boundaries to get the best overall behavior.
